## My thesis provides evidence that can be used for action

:::: incremental
::: {style="font-size: 150%;"}
1.  Integrate temporal heterogeneity and [**historical
    conditions**]{style="color:#006791;"}

2.  Use [**interdisciplinary**]{style="color:#006791;"} approaches and
    perspectives

3.  Assess benefits of [**understudied**]{style="color:#006791;"} types
    of green infrastructure

4.  Contribute a [**multi-scale**]{style="color:#006791;"},
    [**cross-city**]{style="color:#006791;"} study to the Canadian urban
    ecology literature
:::
::::

::: notes
-   cities are temporally dynamics
-   the redevelopment of urban spaces is a social process
:::

## We asked:

:::: incremental
::: {style="font-size: 150%;"}
1.  What are the effects of historical land-use on current park forest
    structure, diversity, and consequently the capacity to provide
    cooling?
2.  How do surrounding communities differ around parks of each
    historical land-use type, and what are the implications for
    equitable access to cooling?
:::
::::

## Past land-use affects park cooling capacity

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="70%"}
![](presentation_imgs/plu_temp_total_plots.png){fig-align="left"
width="90%"}
:::

:::: {.column width="30%"}
::: {layout="[[-1], [1], [-1]]"}
-   Parks cool more during the day
-   Daytime cooling was similar across historical land-use types
-   Previously industrial sites cool less at night
:::
::::
::::::

## Past land-use affects forest structure

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="70%"}
![](presentation_imgs/plu_tree_direct_plots.png){fig-align="left"
width="90%"}
:::

:::: {.column width="30%"}
::: {layout="[[-1], [1], [-1]]"}
-   Previously forested & agricultural sites had the highest mean basal
    area
-   Previously industrial sites had the largest mean tree size
-   Species richness was approximately the same
:::
::::
::::::

## Forest structure affects cooling

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="70%"}
![](presentation_imgs/tree_temp_direct_plots.png){fig-align="left"
width="90%"}
:::

:::: {.column width="30%"}
::: {layout="[[-1], [1], [-1]]"}
-   Relationships between basal area and cooling are dependent on time
    of day and tree size
-   We see little effect of tree size or species richness on cooling for
    large trees
:::
::::
::::::

## Interview results

::::: columns
::: {.column width="40%"}
-   19 ecosystem services mentioned
-   Many of which are cultural
:::

::: {.column width="60%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| label: table-s3

library(scales)
library(dplyr)
library(flextable)

interviews <- read.csv('presentation_imgs/es_coding.csv') %>% 
  select(-c(TotalPeopleMentions))

t <- col_bin("Greens", domain = 0:75)

interviews %>% 
  arrange(desc(TotalMentions)) %>% 
  flextable() %>% 
  bg(
    j = c("TotalMentions"),
    bg = t, part = "body"
  ) %>% 
  set_header_labels(
    EcosystemService = "Ecosystem service",
    TotalMentions = "Total number of mentions"
  ) %>%
  set_table_properties(
    opts_html = list(
      scroll = list(
      height = "500px",
      freeze_first_column = TRUE))
  ) %>% 
  fontsize(size = 18, part = 'all')



```

##  {background-image="presentation_imgs/dogwood.png"}

:::::: {layout="[[-1], [1], [-1]]"}
::::: columns
:::: {.column width="90%"}
::: {style="background-color: #c0c0beff; opacity: 80%"}
-   Green alleys are providing important benefits

-   Different management approaches result in different benefits

    -   Montréal is more variable and also more flexible
    -   TR is less variable but less able to adapt to resident needs

-   Right now, green alleys are providing more biodiversity support than
    ecosystem services with respect to **benefits provided by trees**

-   We recommend a bottom-up approach paired with **expert support** and
    **ongoing funding** to maximize the potential of green alleys
:::
::::
:::::
::::::

![Adapted from Pickett et al. 2017, [Urban
Ecosystems](http://link.springer.com/10.1007/s11252-016-0574-9)](presentation_imgs/adapted-pickett.png){fig-align="center"}

## We asked

:::: incremental
::: {style="font-size: 150%;"}
1.  What is the relative contribution of street trees to predicting
    urban heat and air pollution at different scales when compared to
    urban form and sociodemographics?

2.  What are the relationships between important predictors of
    temperature and air pollution in different cities and across scales?
:::
::::

## We measured temperature, air pollution, ecological form, urban form, and sociodemographics across 7 Canadian cities {.smaller}

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="60%"}
![](presentation_imgs/seven-cities.png){width="80%"}
:::

:::: {.column width="40%"}
::: {layout="[[-1], [1], [-1]]"}
-   Ecosystem service indicator: land surface temperature, air pollution
    (CO, NO2, SO2, UV, O3)

-   Ecological form: street tree diversity/size/density, greenness

-   Urban form: building cover/height, road size/density, greyness

-   Sociodemographics: income, race/ethnicity, immigration status,
    housing
:::
::::
::::::

## We measured our variables at multiple scales {.smaller}

-   Extracted at the most important predictors of temperature and air
    pollution across cities/scales
-   Assessed if there were generalizable patterns

![](presentation_imgs/scale.png){fig-align="center"}

## Predictive models can help us identify areas for further research

:::::: incremental
::::: columns
::: column
-   We need to assess scale-specific interventions for temperature and
    air-pollution related issues in cities

-   Trees are most likely affecting the environmental conditions much
    more than is indicated in this study

-   More multi-scale, multi-service studies are needed in Canada
:::

::: column
![](presentation_imgs/cherry-blossom.jpg){fig-align="right" width="50%"}
:::
:::::
::::::

:::::: {layout="[[-1], [1], [-1]]"}
::::: columns
:::: {.column width="90%"}
::: {style="background-color: #c0c0beff; opacity: 80%"}
**Thesis Take-Aways**

-   Integrating historical conditions facilitates understanding of
    current conditions

-   Spatial scale is of critical importance when discussing nature's
    benefits

-   Small, unconventional green infrastructure types are deserving of
    our attention

-   Interdisciplinary work improves our ability to respond to the needs
    of people
:::

## Interviewee demographics

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| label: interviewees

library(tidyr)

interviewees <- read.csv('presentation_imgs/participant_profiles.csv')

df <- interviewees %>% 
  select(c(Variable, Levels, Count)) %>% 
  drop_na(Count)

df %>% 
  group_by(Variable) %>% 
  mutate(Percent =  round(100 *Count/sum(Count), 0)) %>% 
  ungroup() %>%
  flextable() %>%
  set_table_properties(
  opts_html = list(
    scroll = list(
      height = "500px",
      freeze_first_column = TRUE
    )))

```
